Subject: Scheduling challenge for a multi‑mode, resource‑limited project with timing and budget constraints

Team,

This memo outlines the scheduling challenge for our upcoming project. The work consists of multiple activities that must be sequenced, staffed with renewable resources, and executed under a fixed spending cap. Each activity can be performed in one of several execution modes, trading speed for resource usage and cost. Our goal is to set a feasible plan that finishes as early as possible while honoring all timing rules, avoiding resource conflicts, and staying within budget.

Overview
- The project includes a finite set of activities with defined dependency relationships. Some activities cannot start until others finish, and certain pairs carry explicit minimum and maximum waiting times between completion of the predecessor and the start of the successor.
- Each activity is executed exactly once and cannot be interrupted once it begins. When an activity completes, the resources assigned to it immediately become available for reuse elsewhere.

Execution modes and trade‑offs
- Every activity offers multiple execution modes. Each mode has its own duration, resource usage profile across the renewable resource types, and an associated cost.
- Faster modes shorten activity durations but typically require more resources and higher cost. Slower modes conserve resources and cost but lengthen the timeline.
- We must select one mode for each activity such that the total of all selected mode costs remains within the overall project budget.

Dependencies and timing rules
- Predecessor–successor relationships define the order of work. Certain links require a minimum wait after the predecessor finishes before the successor can start; others additionally impose a maximum allowed wait, beyond which the successor must begin.
- Some activities have earliest permissible start times. A subset has hard completion deadlines that must be met.

Renewable resources and the conservative safety rule
- The project draws on multiple renewable resource types, each with a constant capacity available at all times. Once an activity completes, the resources it used return to the available pool.
- To guard against potential overloads across different execution choices, we will follow a conservative safety rule for activities that are not connected by dependency:
  • If there exists even one combination of their execution modes and one resource type for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, then those two activities will not be allowed to overlap in time. Instead, the schedule must explicitly place one before the other.
  • This safety rule is the only resource management rule in play; there is no separate, continuous capacity check beyond making these pairwise sequencing decisions for potentially conflicting activity pairs.

Budget discipline
- The sum of the costs of the chosen execution modes must not exceed the project’s fixed budget. Mode selections will therefore balance schedule acceleration against financial limits.
- Where the conservative safety rule forces additional sequencing, we may need to adopt faster (and more expensive) modes on key activities to maintain an acceptable completion date, while still respecting the budget cap.

Planning objective and next steps
- The planning objective is to produce a feasible schedule that minimizes the total project duration (makespan) while meeting all dependency rules (including minimum and maximum lags), honoring earliest start times and deadlines, applying the non‑overlap safety rule for resource conflicts, and keeping total mode costs within budget.
- Next, we will: (1) confirm the dependency network and lag limits, (2) validate release dates and deadlines, (3) identify all activity pairs that must be sequenced under the safety rule, and (4) evaluate mode choices that best reduce the timeline without breaching the budget. We will circulate a proposed baseline and critical path once the first pass is complete.

Please review the data summary in the annex and share any corrections or questions prior to baseline development.
